extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / Royal Society members / 17th‑century scientific observers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing a natural history / country report and related observational notes (barometer records, astronomical and meteorological observations, specimen preservation, instrument construction) aimed at early scientific practitioners. Emphasises what particulars to observe, how to record them, and practical methods for experiments and instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometer observation documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be requisite for observers with this instrument to give an account of the situation of the place where the barometers stand; because we may thus not only be capable of judging whether the instruments were duly constructed, but also because the observations may disagree, even when the atmosphere is in the same state, as to weight, if one of them stand in a higher part of the country than the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the exact situation/altitude of the barometer (local height differences can cause 1–3/8 inch differences). Note instrument construction and filling. Report concurrent oddities and exceptions (e.g. short-term drops on a short ride despite fair weather). Observe patterns (Boyle: mercury greatest in droughts, lowest often with high winds) but state caveats: general rules are difficult and may fail. Give comparative readings when possible (same make vs different locations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical and astronomical particulars for a country history
rubrics_metrics.description: To the first sort of particulars belong the longitude and latitude of the place, and consequently the length of the longest and shortest days and nights, the climate, the parallels, &c.; what fixed stars are, and what are not seen there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include precise coordinates and derived astronomical data (day length extremes, visible/absent fixed stars). Use these as foundational data for the natural history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air / atmosphere observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerning the air, may be observed its temperature, as to the first four qualities and the measures of them: its weight, clearness, refractive power; its subtilty or grossness; its abounding with or wanting salts, its variations according to the seasons of the year, and the times of the day; what duration the several kinds of weather usually have; what meteors it mostly produces, and in what order they are generated; and how long they usually last; especially, what winds it is subject to; whether any of them be stated and ordinary, &c. What diseases are epidemical; what is the usual salubrity or insalubrity of the air; and with what constitutions it agrees better or worse than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and describe multiple atmospheric properties (qualitative & quantitative) across seasons and times of day. Record prevailing winds, regular vs occasional winds, typical weather durations, and links between air conditions and local disease/salubrity. Where possible, quantify temperature and weight measures and note refractive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water observations (sea, rivers, lakes, springs, mineral waters, fishes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerning the water, may be observed the sea, its depth, degree of saltness, tides, currents, &c. Next rivers, their width, length, course, inundations, goodness, lightness of waters, &c. Then lakes, ponds, springs, and especially mineral waters, their kinds, qualities, virtues, and how examined. To the waters belong also fishes, their kinds, whether salt or fresh water fish; their quantity, size, goodness, seasons, haunts, peculiarities of any kind, and the ways of taking them, especially those that are not purely mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report physical parameters (depth, salinity, tides, currents), document rivers and inland waters (dimensions, flooding behavior, water quality), and examine mineral waters (identify kinds, test qualities and 'virtues', and describe examination methods). For fisheries, record species, abundance, size, quality, seasonality, habitats, unique behaviors, and capture methods (highlight non-mechanical techniques).

rubrics_metrics.name: Earth / physical geography observations
rubrics_metrics.description: In the earth itself may be observed, its dimensions, situation, east, west, north and south: its figure, its plains and valleys, and their extent; its hills and mountains, and their height; and whether they lie scattered or in ridges, and in what directions they run, &c. What promontories, fiery or smoaking hills, &c. What the magnetical declination is in several places, and the variations of that declination in the same place: what the nature of the soil is, whether clay, sandy, &c. or good mould; and what grains, fruits, and other vegetables, do the most naturally agree with it: also, by what particular arts the inhabitants improve the advantages and remedy the inconveniences of their soil?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe topography, measure and map plains/valleys/hills/mountains (including orientation and ridge patterns), note volcanic or fumarolic features, record compass declination and its local variation, classify soils and associate them with suitable crops/trees, and document local agricultural practices used to exploit or ameliorate the soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inhabitants: physical, social and health particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be given a careful account of the inhabitants themselves, particularly their stature, shape, colour, features, strength, agility, beauty, complexions, hair, diet, inclinations, and customs. Of the women, there may be observed their fruitfulness or barrenness, their hard or easy labour, &c. What diseases both women and men are subject to, and unusual symptoms attending them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide demographic and anthropological descriptions (physical characteristics, health, diet, habits, customs). Include reproductive data for women (fertility, labour conditions) and catalogue common and epidemic diseases with their typical and unusual symptoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: External productions: flora and fauna
rubrics_metrics.description: As to the external productions of the earth, the inquiries may be such as these: What grasses, grains, herbs, flowers, fruit-trees, timber-trees, coppices, groves, woods, forests, &c. What peculiarities are observable in any of them: What soils they best thrive in. What animals the country has, either wild or tame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventory plant life (cultivated and wild), note unique traits, match species to soil types, and list domestic and wild animals. Emphasise particulars valuable for economic or scientific interest (timber, fruit, grasses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal productions: minerals, quarries and mines
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal productions or concealments of the earth, are here understood to be the riches that lie hid under the ground... what sorts of minerals and quarries the country affords, and the particular conditions both of the quarries and the stones: also, how the beds of stone lie, in reference to north and south, &c. What clays and earths it affords, as tobacco pipe-clay, marls, fullers-earths, earths for potters wares, boluses and other medicated earths: What other minerals it yields, as coals, salt-mines, or salt-springs, alum, vitriol, sulphur, &c. What metals the country yields, and a description of the mines, their number, situation, depth, signs, waters, damps, quantities of ore, goodness of ore, extraneous things, and ways of reducing their ores into metals, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey subsurface resources: identify minerals, document quarry characteristics and bed orientations, catalogue useful clays and their uses, report occurrence of salts, vitriol, sulphur, coals, and metals. For mines, record count, locations, depths, indicators/signs, water/damp problems, ore quantities and quality, gangue/extraneous materials, and ore‑processing methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving embryos (birds) taken out of the egg
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to observe the process of nature in the formation of a chick, Mr. Boyle opened the eggs at different periods after incubation, and carefully taking out the embryos, embalmed each of them in spirit of wine in a distinct glass carefully stopped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preserving embryonic specimens: mix a little spirit of sal ammoniac with spirit of wine; first place foetuses in ordinary spirit of wine to wash off loose filth, then transfer to more pure and dephlegmated spirit so the foetus does not discolour it. Embalm each specimen in a separate sealed glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing a compound plano‑convex lens (glass) for longer focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare two glasses, the one exactly flat on both sides, the other flat on one and convex on the other... let them both be put into a ring of brass, and so fastened with cement, that their plane surfaces may be exactly parallel, and the convex side of the plano-convex glass lie inward, so as not to touch the flat of the other. Then fill the space between ... with water, or oil of turpentine, or spirit of wine, or saline liquors, &c, after which stop the hole with a screw. Then, according to the different refraction of the liquors, shall the focus be longer or shorter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble a small plano‑convex lens by pairing a flat–flat glass and a flat–convex glass in a brass ring with parallel planes, filling the gap with liquids that alter refraction (water, oil, alcohol, saline solutions) and sealing the fill hole. Use differing liquids to tune focal length; note that larger sphere lenses and higher‑refractive materials generally produce better spherical optics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving ships from wood‑boring worms
rubrics_metrics.description: There is in the Indian Seas a kind of small worms that fasten themselves to the timber of the ships, and so pierce them that they take in water everywhere; and so weaken the wood, that it is almost impossible to repair them. Many things have been tried to prevent this evil... The Portuguese scorch their ships... but this is dangerous... The most effectual method of preserving the bottoms of ships is that now in use, sheathing them with copper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record attempted remedies and their trade‑offs: lining with deal/hair/lime (retards speed, not fully effective), scorching (dangerous), use of very hard timber (helps), proposed tar from sea coals, and endorses copper sheathing as most effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of a wheel‑barometer to amplify small mercury changes
rubrics_metrics.description: This is only an easy way of applying an index to any common baroscope... by it the variation in the altitude of the mercurial cylinder, which at most is hardly three inches, may be made as distinguishable as if it were three feet, or three yards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe tube (ABC), receiving vessel (IK) dimensions to alter sensitivity: choosing receiver cavity size alters difference amplitude; adjust cylinder width and index length to make smallest variations as sensible as desired. Provide diagrams and proportions to translate small mercury shifts into conspicuous index movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording astronomical planetary spot observations to deduce rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observing a small spot in Jupiter's belt and noting its motion from east to west; measuring its apparent motion (unequal: swifter near center than circumference), diameter and position relative to belts and semidiameter; making ephemerides and using repeated observations across years to compute a period (example: Cassini's period ≈ 9h 55m 58–51s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track identifiable spots repeatedly through the night and across seasons/years; note times of appearance/disappearance, position relative to belts and limb, changes in apparent width (narrow near circumference), and compute periods with attention to observational precision and accounting for observational windows (horizon limits, solar glare). Use multiple observations and ephemerides to estimate revolution counts and period with stated uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and reporting unusual meteorological/optical phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe unusual sky phenomena (e.g. three large circles, parhelia/mock‑suns, colours and relative brightness) with positions, times and geometric relations: diameters, centres, how circles intersect, which has the true sun as centre, colour characteristics and relative luminosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise time of observation, sketch or figure references for geometry (centres, diameters, intersections), describe colours and relative brightness, note positional relations to the sun and horizon, and highlight any parhelias or unusual luminous features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording empirical medical case observations and citing authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Touch and friction have been considered by some as no inefficacious agents in the cure of many diseases and infirmities. (Cites Lord Verulam, Boyle, Piso; reports cases: cure of wen by dead man's hand, warts removed, relief of foot pain by spaniel licking, blacksmith causing vomitings/stools by stroking.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting medical empirical observations: cite prior authorities, describe observed cases in detail (circumstances, practitioner, methods), but note possible alternative explanations (e.g. imagination/placebo effects via absorbent system). Treat extraordinary remedies with caution and consider plausibility and mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative features of a medical treatise (example: Sydenham)
rubrics_metrics.description: The merit of this great physician and original writer consist[s] in his accurate descriptions of what he terms epidemic constitutions; in his history and treatment of the small-pox; and in his rejection of the hot and cordial method of treatment in this eruptive disorder as well as in fevers in general. His theoretical reasonings however are by no means satisfactory; and it has been justly observed by many medical writers, that he carried one part of his cooling method of cure (viz. venesection) to too great a length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value accurate clinical/epidemic description and practical therapeutic guidance over speculative theory. Note strengths and limitations: praise clear observation and effective treatments; critique excessive or unjustified theoretical extensions and overuse of invasive treatments (e.g. excessive venesection).
